title: The Promise of His Coming Stands
summary: Peter answers scoffers who deny Christ’s return, explains God’s patient delay, describes the purging fire of the day of the Lord, and calls believers to holy growth.
historicalContext: Peter writes near the end of his life to congregations that already received his first letter, most likely in the Roman provinces of Asia Minor. Teachers inside the churches were mocking the expectation of Christ’s return. Their argument sounded reasonable in a world where popular philosophy taught that the gods never intervene and that the universe simply continues as it always has: the founders of the faith had died, the seasons still turned, and no judgment had arrived. The denial was more than intellectual. If no Judge was coming, moral restraint could be loosened, and chapter 2 shows how freely these teachers indulged themselves. Some were also bending Paul’s letters, which circulated among these churches, to support their freedom from restraint. Peter answers from the Scriptures the readers already trusted: the creation account, the flood, the psalms, the prophets, the teaching of Jesus, and the apostolic witness.
literaryContext: Chapter 3 completes the argument that began with Peter’s eyewitness testimony and the sure prophetic word (1:16–21) and continued through the exposure of false teachers (chapter 2). The opening call to remember echoes 1:12–15, and the last verse returns to the growth in grace and knowledge with which the letter opened (1:2–8). In between, Peter quotes the scoffers’ question, answers their claim that nothing changes by recalling creation and the flood, and then answers their question about delay by setting God’s view of time and his patient mercy against human impatience. The repeated address “beloved” (vv. 1, 8, 14, 17) marks the movement of the chapter. The description of the day of the Lord is followed at once by moral appeals, so that the hope of the end serves holiness. The closing doxology to Christ rounds off a letter that has defended his power and coming throughout.
themes: Remembering the prophetic and apostolic word
Mockery of the Second Coming and its moral roots
God’s word in creation, flood, and final judgment
Divine patience as an opportunity for repentance
The purging fire and the new heavens and new earth
Holy living and growth while awaiting Christ

outline.title: A Second Reminder
outline.summary: Peter states the purpose of both letters: to rouse sincere minds to remember the prophets and the Lord’s commandment through the apostles.

outline.title: Scoffers Answered from Creation and Flood
outline.summary: Mockers deny Christ’s coming by claiming nothing ever changes, but the word that made the world and flooded it now keeps the present world for fire and judgment.

outline.title: Patient Mercy and the Certain Day
outline.summary: God’s view of time differs from ours; his apparent delay is patience that seeks repentance, yet the day of the Lord will come unexpectedly with fire.

outline.title: Living Toward the New Creation
outline.summary: Expecting a world where righteousness dwells, believers pursue holiness and peace, regard God’s patience as salvation, and refuse the twisting of Paul’s letters and other Scripture.

outline.title: Final Guard and Doxology
outline.summary: Forewarned believers must guard their footing, keep growing in grace and the knowledge of Christ, and give him glory now and forever.

verses.bibleText: This second epistle, beloved, I now write unto you; in both which I stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After the dark catalogue of chapter 2, Peter turns back to his readers with the warm address “beloved,” a word he will repeat at each turning point of this chapter. The false teachers have been exposed; now the faithful are to be strengthened. Calling this “this second epistle” most naturally points to 1 Peter, so that the two letters stand together as one pastor’s counsel to the same churches.

Peter describes both letters as having a single aim: to “stir up” the minds of his readers “by way of remembrance.” He used the same language in 1:13, where he resolved to keep reminding them as long as he lived. Remembering in Scripture is more than recalling information. It means bringing known truth to bear on present choices, the way Israel was told to remember the exodus in order to keep the covenant.

The phrase “pure minds” is a compliment and a guard. The readers’ understanding has not yet been clouded by the teachers who “beguile unstable souls” (2:14). Peter does not offer them novelty. He wants the clear, unmixed thinking they already possess kept clear, alert enough to recognize error when it arrives dressed in reasonable arguments. Truth that is familiar can still fall asleep in the mind, and the apostle’s task is to wake it.

wordNotes.term: εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν (eilikrinē dianoian) — pure minds
wordNotes.explanation: Eilikrinēs describes what is unmixed and therefore sincere, without hidden contamination; dianoia is the thinking mind, the faculty of understanding and judgment. Peter credits his readers with a sincere, uncorrupted way of thinking, set in contrast with the teachers whose minds are governed by desire.

wordNotes.term: ἐν ὑπομνήσει (en hypomnēsei) — by way of remembrance
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase repeats 1:13 and frames the closing chapter as a reminder rather than new instruction. Peter’s method is to bring to the surface what the churches already received, so that settled truth becomes active conviction again.

verses.bibleText: That ye may be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and of the commandment of us the apostles of the Lord and Saviour:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter names what he wants remembered: “the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and … the commandment of us the apostles of the Lord and Saviour.” The two witnesses he defended in chapter 1, the apostolic eyewitnesses on the holy mount and the sure prophetic word, now stand side by side as the church’s foundation. The prophets spoke beforehand of a day when God would judge the earth and renew it. The apostles carried the Lord’s own teaching about his return. Together they form one testimony, and the scoffers of the next verses are rejecting both.

The better-attested Greek reads “your apostles,” meaning the messengers who brought the gospel to these churches, a company that probably included Paul (v. 15). Whatever the wording, the source of the commandment is clear: it belongs to “the Lord and Saviour.” The apostles did not invent it. They delivered it.

“Commandment” in the singular gathers up the whole moral instruction of the gospel, the “holy commandment” from which the false teachers had turned (2:21). Peter will show in this chapter that doctrine and conduct cannot be separated. Those who forget the promised coming soon forget the commandment as well, while those who hold to the prophetic and apostolic word find in it both their hope and their way of life. The church remains itself only as long as it stays built on that foundation.

wordNotes.term: τῶν ἁγίων προφητῶν (tōn hagiōn prophētōn) — the holy prophets
wordNotes.explanation: In light of 1:19–21, these are the Old Testament prophets, whose words were “spoken before” in the sense of announcing what God would do. Their oracles about the day of the Lord and the renewal of creation stand behind everything Peter says in this chapter.

wordNotes.term: ἐντολῆς (entolēs) — commandment
wordNotes.explanation: The singular summarizes the moral teaching Christ gave and the apostles passed on. It links back to “the holy commandment delivered unto them” in 2:21, the standard that apostates abandon and the faithful keep.

verses.bibleText: Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Knowing this first” repeats the opening of 1:20. Before the readers weigh any argument about the future, they should know that its denial was foreseen. Jesus warned of false teachers and of servants who would say in their hearts, “My lord delayeth his coming” (Matthew 24:48). Jude records a similar apostolic prediction. The appearance of scoffers therefore does not disprove the promise; it fulfills a prophecy attached to it.

“The last days” in the New Testament is the whole period opened by Christ’s first coming and the outpouring of the Spirit (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), a period that moves toward its climax. Peter does not speculate about how long it will last. He prepares the church to recognize the spirit of the age whenever it appears, and history has borne out the warning many times.

The scoffers are described before their words are quoted: they walk “after their own lusts.” Peter places the root of their unbelief in their desires. People who want no interference with their appetites have reason to wish that no Judge is coming, and the wish soon becomes a conviction. Their theology follows their conduct. A heart that loves sin cannot long for the return of the sinless Lord, and so it mocks what it does not want to be true. The order matters for every age: skepticism about the Second Coming is often presented as intellectual honesty, but its energy frequently comes from a life that would rather not be examined.

wordNotes.term: ἐμπαῖκται (empaiktai) — scoffers
wordNotes.explanation: The word means mockers, people who ridicule in order to dishonor. Some manuscripts add “in mockery,” intensifying it: they mock with mockery. The verbal form describes the soldiers mocking Jesus before the cross, and the Old Testament often pictures the scorner as proud and morally loose.

wordNotes.term: κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν πορευόμενοι (kata tas idias epithymias autōn poreuomenoi) — walking after their own lusts
wordNotes.explanation: To “walk” is biblical language for a way of life. These people let their own desires set the direction of their conduct, the same trait Peter exposed in 2:10 and 2:18, and that way of life shapes what they are willing to believe.

verses.bibleText: And saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now quotes the scoffers: “Where is the promise of his coming?” The question has a long biblical ancestry. Enemies of God’s people taunted, “Where is now thy God?” (Psalm 42:10), and Jeremiah’s hearers asked, “Where is the word of the LORD? let it come now” (Jeremiah 17:15). Such questions demand visible proof on human terms, and they assume that silence means absence.

“His coming” translates parousia, the word Peter used in 1:16 for the power and coming of Christ that the apostles proclaimed. The scoffers do not attack a minor detail. They target the hope that holds Christian teaching together, because the return of Christ is bound to the resurrection, the judgment, and the restoration of all things.

Their reason is stated: “since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.” “The fathers” most likely refers to the ancestors generally, perhaps the patriarchs of Israel, though some take it as the first generation of believers who had died awaiting Christ. Either way, the argument appeals to the long span of history. Generations have come and gone; nature keeps its regular course; nothing has interrupted it. The claim echoes philosophies of the time that pictured a closed universe untouched by any god.

The phrase “fell asleep” is significant in its own right. Scripture regularly calls death a sleep, an unconscious rest from which the dead will be awakened at Christ’s return (John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–16). The scoffers use the language while denying the event that gives it meaning, for sleep implies waking, and the waking comes with the coming they ridicule. The dead are not presented as already conscious in another realm; they rest until the voice of the returning Lord calls them out.

The argument has a surprisingly modern ring. Confidence in the unbroken uniformity of nature is still offered as a reason to dismiss divine intervention. Peter will answer that the record of history is not as uniform as the scoffers claim.

wordNotes.term: ἡ ἐπαγγελία τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ (hē epangelia tēs parousias autou) — the promise of his coming
wordNotes.explanation: Parousia means arrival or presence and was used of a ruler’s official visit. In the New Testament it often names Christ’s personal return in glory. The “promise” is the whole prophetic and apostolic assurance of that event, which the scoffers treat as empty.

wordNotes.term: ἐκοιμήθησαν (ekoimēthēsan) — fell asleep
wordNotes.explanation: Koimaomai, to sleep, is the common biblical euphemism for death. The image fits Scripture’s teaching that the dead rest unconscious until the resurrection, and it carries the expectation of waking at the Lord’s return.

verses.bibleText: For this they willingly are ignorant of, that by the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter’s reply begins with a charge: “this they willingly are ignorant of.” Their blindness is chosen. The scoffers know the creation story they appeal to, and they know the story of the flood that follows it. They simply refuse to let it count. Paul describes the same deliberate suppression of truth in Romans 1:18–21, where people know God through creation yet do not glorify him.

What they ignore is that the world did not arise or continue on its own. “By the word of God the heavens were of old.” Genesis 1 shows God speaking and creation coming to be, and the psalmist summarizes, “By the word of the LORD were the heavens made” (Psalm 33:6). A world made by a word is not a closed system. It depends at every moment on the One who spoke it into being.

The earth, Peter adds, was “standing out of the water and in the water.” He recalls the creation account in which the earth emerged from the deep and dry land appeared when God gathered the waters (Genesis 1:2, 6–10). He is not offering a scientific description; he is drawing a theological point from the familiar narrative. Water was part of the means by which the earth was formed and held in place.

That detail prepares the next step. The same waters that served creation could be turned, at God’s command, into the instrument of judgment. The scoffers argued from the stability of the world. Peter grants that the world has been stable, then shows that its stability is God’s doing and can be ended by the same authority that sustains it.

wordNotes.term: λανθάνει … θέλοντας (lanthanei … thelontas) — they willingly are ignorant
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “this escapes their notice, as they wish.” The verb describes something slipping past notice, and the participle adds intent. Peter will use the same verb in verse 8 to urge believers not to let God’s view of time escape them.

wordNotes.term: συνεστῶσα (synestōsa) — standing
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect participle pictures the earth as having been formed and continuing to hold together. Colossians uses the same verb of all things holding together in Christ, stressing that creation’s coherence rests on divine power rather than on its own permanence.

verses.bibleText: Whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Whereby” refers back to the waters and the word of verse 5. The waters that God used to form the earth he later used to overwhelm it: “the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished.” Genesis describes the fountains of the deep breaking up and the windows of heaven opening (Genesis 7:11), as if creation’s ordered separation of waters were reversed.

This single event refutes the claim that “all things continue as they were.” Once already, God brought a world to an end in judgment. The “world that then was” refers above all to the ungodly society of Noah’s day and its whole way of life, swept away while Noah and his household were preserved. Peter has used the flood twice before (1 Peter 3:20; 2 Peter 2:5), and Jesus himself made it the pattern of his coming: people ate, drank, and married “until the flood came, and took them all away” (Matthew 24:39). The scoffers had forgotten the very precedent that answers them.

wordNotes.term: κατακλυσθεὶς ἀπώλετο (kataklystheis apōleto) — being overflowed with water, perished
wordNotes.explanation: Kataklyzō means to flood or deluge and appears only here in the New Testament. Apollymi means to destroy or ruin. Together they describe the antediluvian world brought to an end, an example of complete judgment rather than a mild correction.

verses.bibleText: But the heavens and the earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now draws the conclusion. “The heavens and the earth, which are now” stand alongside “the world that then was” (v. 6). The letter thinks in three worlds: the world before the flood, the present world, and the new heavens and new earth still to come (v. 13). The same word that created the first world and ended it in water now governs the second.

This present world is “kept in store, reserved unto fire.” The language is of something stored up and guarded for an appointed purpose. The stability the scoffers point to is real, but it is not evidence that nothing will change. It is God holding the present order for a coming day. In chapter 2 Peter used the same idea of the angels who sinned and of the unjust, who are “reserved unto judgment” (2:4, 9). Divine providence does not compete with divine judgment; it leads toward it.

The means will be fire rather than water. God promised Noah that a flood would never again destroy the earth (Genesis 9:11), and the prophets repeatedly picture the final judgment as burning (Isaiah 66:15–16; Malachi 4:1). Sodom, reduced to ashes (2:6), already served as a preview.

The target of that fire is named with care: “the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men.” Matter is not the real object of judgment. People are. “Perdition” translates the same word Peter used for the “swift destruction” the false teachers bring on themselves (2:1). Scripture describes the end of the wicked as destruction, a fire that leaves “neither root nor branch” (Malachi 4:1), not as an unending life in torment. The fire that judges the ungodly is the fire that removes sin from God’s universe, so that a clean creation can follow.

wordNotes.term: τεθησαυρισμένοι … τηρούμενοι (tethēsaurismenoi … tēroumenoi) — kept in store … reserved
wordNotes.explanation: The first participle comes from the verb for storing up treasure; the second means kept or guarded. Both picture the present creation as held by God for a fixed purpose. The perfect tense of the first suggests a settled condition that continues until the appointed day.

wordNotes.term: ἀπωλείας (apōleias) — perdition
wordNotes.explanation: Apōleia means destruction or ruin, the opposite of salvation. Peter uses it for the end of the false teachers (2:1, 3) and of those who twist Scripture (3:16). It describes final loss, the end of existence apart from God.

verses.bibleText: But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With “But, beloved” Peter turns from the scoffers to the faithful. The verb is the one used in verse 5: the mockers chose to let a truth escape them, and believers must not let this “one thing” slip from their notice. The contrast is pointed. One group reasons from impatience; the other is to reason from Scripture.

The truth he gives comes from Moses’ prayer in Psalm 90: “a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past” (Psalm 90:4). That psalm sets the brevity of human life against the eternity of God and asks for a heart that numbers its days wisely. Peter adds the reverse clause, “one day is with the Lord as a thousand years,” so that the comparison runs both ways. God is not bound by the measures of time that make waiting feel long to us. A thousand years do not weary him, and a single day is never too short for him to accomplish what he intends.

The point answers the complaint about delay. What looks long to a generation that wants immediate proof is not long in the reckoning of the eternal God. Human impatience is not a fair measure of divine faithfulness.

The context also limits what the verse means. Peter is not giving a formula for converting days into millennia, nor a key for calculating the date of Christ’s return. Later writers built schemes from this verse, dividing world history into six thousand-year days followed by a millennial rest, but Peter offers no such timetable. Where prophecy uses symbolic time, Scripture supplies its own pattern in its own passages (Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6); this verse belongs to a different argument. Jesus said plainly that no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36). The verse rebukes impatience with God; it does not license impatience to compute what he has kept to himself. Its practical effect is trust: the believer can leave the timing with God and give attention to readiness.

wordNotes.term: μὴ λανθανέτω (mē lanthanetō) — be not ignorant
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “let it not escape your notice.” The same verb in verse 5 described the willful ignorance of the scoffers. Peter sets the two side by side: what they choose to overlook, believers must keep firmly in view.

wordNotes.term: ὡς χίλια ἔτη (hōs chilia etē) — as a thousand years
wordNotes.explanation: The comparative “as” signals likeness, not an exact equivalence. Drawn from Psalm 90:4, the expression contrasts God’s eternal perspective with human reckoning and does not supply a numerical conversion for prophetic dates.

verses.bibleText: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here Peter gives the heart of his answer. “The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness.” The scoffers interpret the passing of time as negligence, as if God had forgotten or could not act. The word Peter uses means to delay or loiter, and Habakkuk had already heard the assurance that the vision “will surely come, it will not tarry” (Habakkuk 2:3). The promise is on God’s schedule, not ours, and it will not fail.

What looks like delay is something else: he “is longsuffering to us-ward.” Longsuffering is the patience that holds back deserved judgment. It belongs to the self-description God gave Moses, “merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). The same patience waited in the days of Noah while the ark was being prepared (1 Peter 3:20). The time between the promise and its fulfillment is the space God’s mercy has opened.

The better-supported reading is “toward you.” Peter is reminding the church that it owes its own salvation to this patience. Many in those congregations, and many who read the letter since, came to Christ during the very period the scoffers called proof of God’s absence. The time is also a call to those wavering under the false teachers’ influence: the door is still open.

The reason for the patience is God’s desire: “not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.” The verb expresses what God wishes, his inclination of heart. It agrees with Ezekiel, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11), and with Paul, who says God “will have all men to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4). God has not selected some for destruction by arbitrary decree. His will toward every person is life.

Yet the verse does not teach that all will be saved. Repentance must be received, and the same chapter speaks of the “perdition of ungodly men” (v. 7). God does not force the will. His patience creates opportunity, and opportunity can be refused. The delay therefore cuts two ways: it is mercy to all who turn, and it is a warning to all who presume on it, because patience has an end.

wordNotes.term: μακροθυμεῖ εἰς ὑμᾶς (makrothymei eis hymas) — is longsuffering to us-ward
wordNotes.explanation: Makrothymeō means to be slow to anger, to bear patiently with offenders. The better manuscripts read “toward you,” addressing the readers directly. God’s restraint is directed at the church and through it at the world, giving time for repentance.

wordNotes.term: μὴ βουλόμενος (mē boulomenos) — not willing
wordNotes.explanation: Boulomai often expresses desire or intention of heart. God does not want anyone to perish. The phrase describes his gracious will toward all people, not a guarantee that every person will accept it, since repentance is required.

verses.bibleText: But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But the day of the Lord will come.” In the Greek the verb stands first for emphasis: come it will. God’s patience is real, but it is not indefinite. The “day of the Lord” is the prophets’ phrase for God’s decisive intervention to judge and to save (Joel 2:31; Zephaniah 1:14–18), and the New Testament links it with the return of Christ.

It will come “as a thief in the night.” Jesus used the image (Matthew 24:43), and Paul and John repeated it (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 16:15). The point of comparison is unexpectedness. A thief gives no notice, and those who are unprepared are caught off guard. The image has nothing to do with secrecy or invisibility. The same verse describes the heavens passing away “with a great noise,” and elsewhere Scripture insists that every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7) and that his coming will be as visible as lightning across the sky (Matthew 24:27). Only the timing is hidden; the event will be public, audible, and universal. Because it comes suddenly, readiness cannot be postponed until it arrives.

Peter then describes the end of the present order. The heavens “pass away with a great noise,” a rushing roar such as fire makes. “The elements shall melt with fervent heat.” The elements are most naturally the material components of the world, which will be broken down in the burning. The language gathers up the prophets’ pictures of mountains melting before the Lord (Micah 1:4) and of a day that burns as an oven (Malachi 4:1).

The final clause has a well-known textual question. Many later manuscripts read “shall be burned up,” but some of the oldest read “shall be found,” meaning laid bare before God. The two readings agree in substance. Nothing on earth will escape exposure and judgment; every work will be revealed for what it is, and all that is evil will be consumed.

The fire is purposeful. Revelation places the final fire at the close of the thousand years, when it consumes the wicked and their works (Revelation 20:9), and it is followed by a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1). Peter says the same in verse 13. The burning ends sin; it does not perpetuate it. What God made, he does not abandon. He cleanses it, so that a new creation free from every trace of evil can replace what sin had ruined.

wordNotes.term: ῥοιζηδόν (rhoizēdon) — with a great noise
wordNotes.explanation: This rare adverb imitates a rushing, whizzing sound, like the beat of wings or something hurtling through the air. Here it probably evokes the roar of flames or the thunder of God’s appearing, making clear that the day of the Lord is anything but quiet or hidden.

wordNotes.term: στοιχεῖα (stoicheia) — elements
wordNotes.explanation: The word originally meant things set in a row, such as letters of the alphabet, and came to mean the basic components of a thing. In this context it most likely refers to the physical constituents of the world, which will be broken up and melted in the purging fire.

verses.bibleText: Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now turns from the event to the people who expect it. “Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved” gathers up verses 7–10. If the present order is destined for dissolution, then what kind of life makes sense now? The question is rhetorical and carries the force of a command.

“What manner of persons ought ye to be” shows where Peter’s interest lies. He has described the end, but he is not writing a cosmology. His concern is character. The word for “what manner” asks about quality, the kind of people the readers are becoming, and the verb “ought” expresses moral necessity. Knowledge of the end leaves no room for indifference.

The answer is “all holy conversation and godliness.” In the Greek both nouns are plural, as if Peter wanted to cover every kind of conduct and every act of devotion. “Conversation” in the KJV means manner of life, the whole pattern of behavior visible to others. “Godliness” is reverent devotion to God shown in practice, a word that frames the letter from its opening (1:3, 6–7).

The logic is the reverse of the scoffers’. They reasoned that because no judgment is coming, restraint is unnecessary. Peter reasons that because the world will be dissolved, only what belongs to God will last. Possessions, reputations, and pleasures built on this order will pass with it. Holiness is the one investment that carries over into the new creation.

wordNotes.term: ποταποὺς δεῖ ὑπάρχειν ὑμᾶς (potapous dei hyparchein hymas) — what manner of persons ought ye to be
wordNotes.explanation: Potapos asks about the quality or character of a person, not merely their type. With dei, “it is necessary,” the question becomes an urgent appeal: those who know the end must be people of a certain kind now.

wordNotes.term: ἐν ἁγίαις ἀναστροφαῖς καὶ εὐσεβείαις (en hagiais anastrophais kai eusebeiais) — in all holy conversation and godliness
wordNotes.explanation: Anastrophē means way of life; eusebeia means devotion to God shown in conduct. Both are plural, embracing every area of behavior and every act of reverence. Peter’s first letter uses anastrophē repeatedly for the conduct that commends the gospel to observers.

verses.bibleText: Looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of God, wherein the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The holy life of verse 11 has a forward lean: “looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of God.” The first participle describes eager, confident expectation. It is the verb used of people waiting for someone whose arrival is certain. Peter uses it three times in three verses (vv. 12–14), so that the whole posture of the church is one of expectation.

The second participle is harder. “Hasting unto” can mean earnestly desiring, but with a direct object the verb more naturally means hastening or speeding something on. Peter then appears to say that believers can hasten the coming of the day of God. That fits verse 9: if God delays because he is waiting for repentance, then the repentance of sinners and the proclamation that calls them to it move history toward its goal. Jesus said that the gospel of the kingdom would be preached in all the world, “and then shall the end come” (Matthew 24:14). In Acts 3:19–20 Peter himself linked repentance with the times of refreshing and the sending of Christ.

This does not mean that the church controls God’s timetable or that the date can be engineered. God remains sovereign over the day (Acts 1:7). But the church is not a passive spectator. By holy living, faithful witness, and prayer for the kingdom’s coming, it participates in the purpose for which the delay exists.

Peter then repeats the description of verse 10: “the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat.” The present tense of “melt” makes the picture vivid. The repetition is deliberate. The day that dissolves the old order is the day believers long for, because they know what follows. Fire is not their final word; it clears the ground for the new heavens and new earth that the next verse announces. For the believer, longing for that day is longing for the end of sin, suffering, and death.

wordNotes.term: προσδοκῶντας (prosdokōntas) — looking for
wordNotes.explanation: Prosdokaō means to wait for with expectation, used of anticipating someone sure to arrive. Repeated in verses 12, 13, and 14, it describes the settled, eager outlook of believers in contrast with the scoffers’ dismissal.

wordNotes.term: σπεύδοντας (speudontas) — hasting unto
wordNotes.explanation: Speudō means to hurry, and with an object, to hasten something on; in classical Greek it could also mean to desire earnestly. Here it suggests that believers, by repentance, holy living, and gospel witness, take part in bringing the day near, without implying that they set its time.

verses.bibleText: Nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Nevertheless” turns the scene from fire to hope. The burning is not the end of the story. “We, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.” The scoffers asked, “Where is the promise?” (v. 4). Peter answers by naming its content and declaring that he and the church still expect it.

The promise comes from Isaiah: “behold, I create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). Isaiah pictures a world without weeping, where people build and inhabit, plant and eat, and where the wolf and the lamb feed together. Jesus spoke of “the regeneration” (Matthew 19:28) and promised that the meek would inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). John saw “a new heaven and a new earth,” with God dwelling among his people and death removed (Revelation 21:1–4).

The word for “new” describes newness of kind and quality, not merely recent appearance. The coming creation is this world made new, cleansed of sin and restored to what God intended, not a vague spiritual realm detached from the physical. The redeemed will live in bodies raised from the dead on an earth renewed by the Creator. The fire of verses 10–12 serves this purpose: it removes what corrupts so that what is good can be established for ever.

Its defining mark is that righteousness “dwelleth” there. The verb means to settle and make one’s home. In the present world righteousness is often a stranger, resisted and outnumbered; in the new earth it will be the permanent resident. This is why the hope purifies. People who long for a home where righteousness lives begin to welcome righteousness into their lives now.

wordNotes.term: καινοὺς δὲ οὐρανοὺς καὶ γῆν καινήν (kainous de ouranous kai gēn kainēn) — new heavens and a new earth
wordNotes.explanation: Kainos stresses newness of quality, what is fresh and different in kind. The phrase repeats Isaiah’s promise and points to the present creation renewed and freed from sin, a real heaven and earth fitted for the resurrected people of God.

wordNotes.term: κατοικεῖ (katoikei) — dwelleth
wordNotes.explanation: Katoikeō means to settle down and live permanently in a place, as opposed to staying temporarily. Righteousness is pictured as the lasting inhabitant of the new creation, at home there in a way it never is in a world under sin.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore” draws the practical conclusion from the hope just stated. Those who “look for such things” must “be diligent.” Peter used the same verb in 1:10, urging his readers to give diligence to make their calling and election sure. Expectation is never idle. It calls for effort, energy, and attention.

The goal is “that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.” “Found” suggests examination: when Christ comes, he will look at what his people are. The prospect of meeting him face to face is what motivates the preparation.

“Without spot, and blameless” deliberately reverses the description of the false teachers as “spots … and blemishes” (2:13). It also echoes Peter’s first letter, where Christ is the “lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:19). The people of the spotless Lamb are to reflect his purity. This is not a call to earn acceptance by moral achievement. The blamelessness Peter has in mind grows from the grace and knowledge of Christ (1:2–8) and is the fruit of the Spirit’s work in those whom Christ has cleansed.

“In peace” is the condition in which believers should be found. It is first peace with God, the reconciliation that comes through justification (Romans 5:1), and then the settled confidence and harmony that follow. Those who live in that peace need not dread the day of God. They can welcome it as the arrival of the Friend they have been expecting. Readiness for that meeting is built in ordinary days, through confession, reconciliation, and faithful obedience.

wordNotes.term: ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἀμώμητοι (aspiloi kai amōmētoi) — without spot, and blameless
wordNotes.explanation: The pair negates the words used for the false teachers in 2:13, “spots and blemishes.” Both terms describe moral and spiritual purity, the condition of those who belong to Christ, the unblemished Lamb, and are shaped by his grace.

wordNotes.term: σπουδάσατε (spoudasate) — be diligent
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to make every effort or to be zealous. It is one of Peter’s characteristic words in this letter (1:10, 15), expressing the urgency of preparing for Christ’s coming rather than waiting carelessly.

verses.bibleText: And account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation; even as our beloved brother Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter returns to the theme of verse 9 with a command: “account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation.” The scoffers counted the delay as slackness. Believers are to evaluate the same facts differently. The time that has passed since the promise is not evidence of God’s weakness but the space in which salvation is being offered and received. The patience of the Lord is not itself salvation, but it makes salvation possible for all who will turn.

“Our Lord” most likely refers to Christ, the one whose coming is in question. The Saviour who will return in judgment is the same one who restrains judgment so that more may be rescued.

Peter then appeals to “our beloved brother Paul.” The phrase shows real fellowship between the two apostles, despite the public rebuke Paul once gave Peter at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). Peter does not cling to wounded pride. He calls Paul beloved and acknowledges that he wrote “according to the wisdom given unto him.” The wisdom was given, not self-produced. Paul himself said that his message came by revelation and the Spirit’s teaching (1 Corinthians 2:12–13).

Paul had written to these churches on the same theme. His letters speak repeatedly of God’s patience leading to repentance (Romans 2:4) and of holy living in view of Christ’s return (1 Thessalonians 5:1–11). By aligning himself with Paul, Peter undercuts the false teachers, who appear to have claimed Paul’s support for their views.

wordNotes.term: μακροθυμίαν … σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθε (makrothymian … sōtērian hēgeisthe) — account that the longsuffering … is salvation
wordNotes.explanation: Hēgeomai means to consider or regard. Peter uses the same verb in verse 9 for the scoffers who “count” it slackness. Believers are told to make the opposite judgment, regarding God’s forbearance as the opportunity for salvation.

wordNotes.term: κατὰ τὴν δοθεῖσαν αὐτῷ σοφίαν (kata tēn dotheisan autō sophian) — according to the wisdom given unto him
wordNotes.explanation: The passive “given” points to God as the source of Paul’s wisdom. Peter recognizes Paul’s writings as the product of divine gift, consistent with Paul’s own claim to speak by the Spirit rather than by human cleverness.

verses.bibleText: As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter widens the reference: Paul speaks “of these things” not in one letter only but “in all his epistles.” The coming of Christ, the judgment, God’s patience, and the call to holiness run through Paul’s writings. Peter’s remark implies that a collection of Paul’s letters was already circulating and being read in the churches.

Peter admits frankly that Paul’s letters contain “some things hard to be understood.” Not everything is difficult, but some things are. Even an apostle found parts of Paul demanding, and that candor is a comfort to every reader who has struggled with Romans or Galatians. Difficulty is not the problem. The problem is what certain people do with it.

“They that are unlearned and unstable wrest” these passages. The unlearned are those untaught in the faith, who lack a grasp of the whole of God’s revelation; the unstable are those without firm footing, easily swept along (2:14). To “wrest” is to twist, as on a rack, forcing a meaning out of a text that it was never meant to bear. Paul’s own letters show what was being twisted. Some turned his teaching on grace into a license for sin, a slander he answered directly: “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid” (Romans 6:1–2). He insisted that faith does not make void the law but establishes it (Romans 3:31). Others distorted his teaching on the Lord’s coming, claiming the day had already arrived (2 Thessalonians 2:2). Both errors match the false teachers of 2 Peter, who promised liberty and mocked the coming judgment.

They do this “as they do also the other scriptures.” The phrase places Paul’s letters alongside the Old Testament as Scripture. Peter, who in 1:20–21 defended the divine origin of prophecy, here recognizes apostolic writing as carrying the same authority.

The twisting leads “unto their own destruction.” Scripture is given to make people wise unto salvation (2 Timothy 3:15). Bent to serve desire, it becomes the means of self-deception. The remedy Peter implies is to read difficult passages in harmony with the plain teaching of the whole Bible, letting Scripture interpret Scripture.

wordNotes.term: δυσνόητα (dysnoēta) — hard to be understood
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective means difficult to grasp and occurs only here in the New Testament. Peter says “some things” are hard, not everything. The difficulty calls for patient, humble study within the whole teaching of Scripture.

wordNotes.term: στρεβλοῦσιν (streblousin) — wrest
wordNotes.explanation: Strebloō means to twist or torture, as on a rack. The image is of forcing a passage to say what it does not mean. Peter applies it both to Paul’s letters and to the rest of Scripture.

verses.bibleText: Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The emphatic “Ye therefore, beloved” separates the readers from the unlearned and unstable of verse 16. They have been warned, “seeing ye know these things before.” The letter itself, along with the words of prophets and apostles, has given them advance notice of the error and its methods. Forewarned, they are responsible to be forearmed.

“Beware lest ye also … fall from your own stedfastness.” Peter does not assume that the faithful are beyond danger. Being “led away” describes being swept along with others, the same verb used of Barnabas carried away by hypocrisy at Antioch (Galatians 2:13). Error spreads socially as well as intellectually. “The error of the wicked” refers to the lawless, those who reject moral restraint, the same word Peter used for the people of Sodom (2:7).

“Stedfastness” is a firm footing, the opposite of the “unstable” in verse 16. It is real, and it can be lost. Yet Peter does not leave his readers anxious. The God who calls them is able to keep them from falling (Jude 1:24), and the next verse shows how that keeping works in practice.

wordNotes.term: προγινώσκοντες (proginōskontes) — seeing ye know these things before
wordNotes.explanation: The participle means knowing in advance. Peter’s readers have been given warning ahead of time through the prophetic and apostolic word and through this letter, so that the error should not take them by surprise.

wordNotes.term: τοῦ ἰδίου στηριγμοῦ (tou idiou stērigmou) — your own stedfastness
wordNotes.explanation: Stērigmos means firm position or stability. It contrasts with astēriktoi, “unstable,” in verse 16, and echoes Peter’s wish that the readers be “established in the present truth” (1:12).

verses.bibleText: But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter’s final command answers the danger of verse 17. The antidote to falling is growing: “But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.” The present tense means keep on growing. Christian life never reaches a point where it can stand still without beginning to slide.

Growth in grace means deeper experience of God’s undeserved favor and power, which both forgives and transforms. Growth in knowledge means a fuller personal acquaintance with Christ, who he is and what he does, the knowledge the letter has emphasized from its opening verses (1:2–3, 8). Peter’s first letter urged believers to desire the word so that they might grow (1 Peter 2:2); his second ends by naming the goal of that growth, Jesus Christ himself.

The letter closes with a doxology addressed to Christ: “To him be glory both now and for ever.” Few New Testament doxologies are directed explicitly to the Son, and this one confirms the high view of Christ that opened the letter, where he is called “God and our Saviour” (1:1). The phrase “for ever” is literally “unto the day of eternity,” the day that begins with his coming and never ends. The glory begins now, in lives that honor him while they wait.

wordNotes.term: αὐξάνετε (auxanete) — grow
wordNotes.explanation: The present imperative calls for continual increase. The same verb appears in 1 Peter 2:2 for newborn believers growing by the milk of the word. Here it applies to the whole church, which is to keep advancing in grace and in the knowledge of Christ.

wordNotes.term: εἰς ἡμέραν αἰῶνος (eis hēmeran aiōnos) — for ever
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “unto the day of eternity.” The unusual phrase links the doxology with the day of the Lord described in this chapter: the day that ends the old order begins an age of unending glory for Christ.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: When a promise seems long in coming, what decides whether we keep trusting the one who made it?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The God whose word created and judged the world will keep his promise of Christ’s return; his delay is mercy, and his coming calls for holy, growing lives that look forward to the new earth.
importantTerms: new heavens and a new earth
discussionQuestions: How does Peter connect the scoffers’ desires with their denial of Christ’s coming?
Why does the flood answer the claim that “all things continue as they were”?
What does verse 9 reveal about God’s character and about the reason for the delay?
How should expecting a world “wherein dwelleth righteousness” shape ordinary conduct now?
What safeguards does Peter give against twisting difficult parts of Scripture?
commonMisunderstandings: Verse 8 is not a formula for calculating the date of Christ’s return or for building a scheme of world history.
The thief image stresses suddenness for the unprepared; it does not describe a secret or invisible coming.
The fire of the last day ends sin and sinners; it does not preserve the wicked in endless torment.
God’s wish that none should perish does not mean that all will be saved regardless of their response.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the certainty of the promise and the patience of God together, and let both lead to holiness, witness, and steady growth in Christ.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Receive God’s patience as your opportunity, turn from whatever would leave you unready, and live today as a citizen of the new earth that Christ is coming to bring.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Christ will return visibly to judge the world, God delays in patient love so that sinners may repent, and he will make a new earth where righteousness dwells.
flow: Many doubt Christ’s return because life seems to go on unchanged.
Scripture shows that God has acted in history before, at creation and in the flood.
The time that has passed reveals God’s patience, not his forgetfulness.
The day of the Lord will come suddenly and will end sin by fire.
God promises a new heavens and a new earth, and he invites everyone to repent and be ready.
simpleIllustrations: A rescue boat that waits at a flooded village is not late; it stays because some people have not yet come out.
A gardener burns away weeds and thorns so that the field can be planted again; the fire serves the new crop.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you accept God’s patience as your opportunity and give your life to Christ before he comes?
cautions: Do not set or suggest dates for the Second Coming.
Do not describe the final fire as an endless torment of conscious souls.
Do not use fear alone; present God’s patient love and the hope of the new earth.

reflectionQuestions: Where have I let the apparent delay of Christ’s coming make me careless or doubtful?
Do I see God’s patience with me as an opportunity I am using or one I am wasting?
What in my life would I want gone before Christ finds me, and what should I begin now?
How am I growing in grace and in the knowledge of Jesus Christ this season?
Which teaching or influence around me might be loosening my steadfastness?
